chapters.title: Master Your Emotional Self: The Law of Irrationality
chapters.keys: You are not as rational as you think, and neither is anyone else; emotions bend your thinking all day, and the first step is to admit it. Greene splits the problem into low-grade irrationality, the steady background biases that tilt every judgment, such as seeing only what confirms your view or blaming others, and high-grade irrationality, the flare-ups when anger, fear or greed take over completely. He names the inflaming factors that set off the second kind: old triggers from early life, sudden gains or losses, rising pressure, inflaming individuals, and the pull of a group. His method runs in three steps: first recognize your biases, then watch for the inflaming factors, then work to bring out your rational self by knowing yourself well, tracing your emotions to their roots, giving yourself more time before you react, accepting people as facts instead of wishing they were different, finding the balance where thought and feeling work together, and learning to love reason itself. The aim is not to kill emotion but to see it clearly, so it stops steering you blind. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Pericles led Athens with calm, steady reason and kept the city on a careful course, but after he died in the plague, leaders driven by passion took over and Athens lurched into reckless ventures, above all the Sicilian expedition, which ended in disaster.

chapters.title: Transform Self-love into Empathy: The Law of Narcissism
chapters.keys: Everyone is self-absorbed, and that is not the problem; the problem is when your self-love stays turned inward. Greene places people on a narcissistic spectrum, from the deep narcissist, who has no real sense of self and feeds on others' attention, to the healthy narcissist, whose solid self lets attention flow outward. Learn to spot deep narcissists early and keep away from them, and turn your own self-love into empathy. His tools come in order: the empathic attitude, assuming you do not yet understand the other person; visceral empathy, catching their mood and feeling; analytic empathy, learning their history and values; and the empathic skill, testing and correcting your reading through practice. Empathy, he says, is a skill built by turning attention outward, and it gives you power over people because you see what they want and fear. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Greene shows Leo and Sonya Tolstoy locked in a marriage of two narcissists who could not see each other, and Ernest Shackleton, whose close reading of each man's moods held his crew together after their ship Endurance was crushed in the ice, until all of them were brought home alive.

chapters.title: See Through People's Masks: The Law of Role-playing
chapters.keys: People wear masks and present the face they want you to see, so stop trusting words and learn to read what leaks out underneath. Watch the nonverbal cues: the face, the voice, the posture, the small slips that show what someone really feels. Greene sorts these into decoding keys: signs of like or dislike, signs of dominance or submission, and signs of deception. Then use the same knowledge on yourself through impression management, the deliberate shaping of how others see you, playing your role well instead of being caught by it. He argues it works because people constantly give away their true feelings through the body, and almost nobody pays close attention. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Milton Erickson, paralyzed by polio as a teenager and able only to watch his family, learned to read the hidden meanings in faces, voices and gestures, and later built a career as a psychiatrist on that skill.

chapters.title: Determine the Strength of People's Character: The Law of Compulsive Behavior
chapters.keys: Judge people by their character, not by their charm, their talent or what they say about themselves. Character is the set of deep patterns laid down early in life, and people repeat those patterns over and over; past behavior is the best guide to what someone will do. Look at how they act under stress, how they handle power, and what they do in small moments when they think no one is watching. Greene describes toxic types to avoid, among them the hyperperfectionist, the relentless rebel, the personalizer, the drama magnet, the big talker, the pampered prince or princess and the pleaser. Know your own character too, so you can strengthen its good side and stop being ruled by its compulsions. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Howard Hughes, despite great talent and wealth, kept wrecking his own projects by insisting on total control, a pattern he repeated across his life until he ended isolated.

chapters.title: Become an Elusive Object of Desire: The Law of Covetousness
chapters.keys: People want what they cannot have, and they lose interest in what is easy to get. Do not make yourself too available; keep some mystery, hold something back, and withdraw at the right moment so others come looking for you. Greene's tools include creating a sense of scarcity, stirring rivalry and the sense that others want what you have, using the pull of what is forbidden or out of reach, and leaving gaps that people fill with their own fantasies. Know that the same hunger for the absent works on you, and learn to value what you already have. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Coco Chanel, an orphan raised in poverty, built a fashion empire by shaping desire, keeping herself mysterious and making her designs and perfume feel rare and hard to get.

chapters.title: Elevate Your Perspective: The Law of Shortsightedness
chapters.keys: People get swept up in what is happening right now and lose sight of where events are heading. Train yourself to step back and take the long view, judging today's events by their likely consequences months and years ahead. Greene names the signs of shortsightedness: unintended consequences, acting without thinking through the chain of effects; tactical hell, being caught in endless small battles; ticker-tape fever, reacting to every bit of news; and lost in trivia, drowning in details while missing the larger picture. Raise your perspective by keeping long-term goals in front of you and refusing to react in the heat of the moment. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: John Blunt of the South Sea Company devised a scheme to turn the national debt into company shares, which set off a buying mania until the bubble burst and ruined many investors; Isaac Newton bought into the company and sold at a profit, but as the mania grew he bought back in near the top and lost a fortune when the bubble burst.

chapters.title: Soften People's Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion: The Law of Defensiveness
chapters.keys:
Soften People's Resistance by Confirming Their Self-opinion: The Law of Defensiveness
People resist being pushed, so stop arguing and start making them feel good about themselves. Everyone holds a self-opinion, a flattering picture of themselves as independent, intelligent and good, and anything that threatens it makes them defensive. Confirm that picture and their guard comes down. Greene's strategies for the master persuader: become a deep listener; infect people with the right mood; confirm their self-opinion; ease their insecurities; and use their resistance and stubbornness instead of fighting it. Turn the same insight on yourself by keeping your own mind flexible and open instead of defending your positions. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Lyndon Johnson came to the Senate as a junior member and rose to majority leader by listening, deferring to and building up powerful senators, above all Richard Russell, who in return backed him.

chapters.title: Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude: The Law of Self-sabotage
chapters.keys:
Change Your Circumstances by Changing Your Attitude: The Law of Self-sabotage
Your attitude, the way you habitually see the world, shapes what happens to you, and a negative attitude quietly sabotages you. Greene contrasts the constricted attitude, which narrows what you see out of fear and closes you off, with the expansive attitude, which opens you to people and possibilities. He names constricted attitudes, among them the hostile, the anxious, the avoidant, the depressive and the resentful, and shows how each draws the very circumstances it fears. Change the lens and your circumstances change with it: see adversity as a chance to learn, see others with understanding, and see yourself as able to grow. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Anton Chekhov grew up poor under a brutal father, and instead of staying bitter he chose to see his father with understanding, freed himself from resentment, and went on to become a great writer even while ill with tuberculosis.

chapters.title: Confront Your Dark Side: The Law of Repression
chapters.keys:
Confront Your Dark Side: The Law of Repression
Everyone has a dark side, the shadow, made of the traits and impulses we bury because they do not fit the image we want to show. Buried, it does not go away; it leaks out in ways that hurt you and others. Greene lists the signs of the shadow: contradictory behavior, sudden emotional outbursts, vehement denial, accident-prone behavior, overidealizing people or causes, and projection, seeing in others what you deny in yourself. Look for these in others and in yourself. Then see your shadow, accept it, explore it, and show parts of it openly, so its energy works for you instead of against you. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Richard Nixon presented a controlled, upright public face while keeping his resentments and suspicions hidden, and that buried side broke out in the Watergate scandal that ended his presidency.

chapters.title: Beware the Fragile Ego: The Law of Envy
chapters.keys:
Beware the Fragile Ego: The Law of Envy
Envy is everywhere and nobody admits to it, so it comes out hidden and disguised. Learn to see it early: look for flashes of resentment in the face, praise with a poisoned edge, gossip behind your back, and friends who pull close then turn cold. Greene describes types of enviers, among them the leveler, who drags everyone down; the entitled slacker; the status fiend; the attacher, who clings to successful people; and the insecure master, the boss threatened by talented people beneath them. Avoid stirring envy by not flaunting your success and by showing your flaws, and deal with envy in yourself by turning it into admiration and the drive to improve. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: In Italy, Mary Shelley and her husband Percy became friends with Edward and Jane Williams, but Jane envied Mary's fame and intelligence and, while still acting as her friend, spread lies about her. After a boating accident drowned Percy and Edward, Jane turned cold, and Mary ended the friendship.

chapters.title: Know Your Limits: The Law of Grandiosity
chapters.keys:
Know Your Limits: The Law of Grandiosity
Success goes to people's heads; they start to think they are more powerful and gifted than they are and take reckless risks. Greene calls this grandiosity, an inflated sense of self that grows with success and attention. Watch for it in leaders and in yourself: a sense of being untouchable, contempt for advice, overreach. Do not kill the energy behind it; turn it into practical grandiosity, ambition kept tied to reality, by honestly assessing what part luck and others played in your success, staying focused on the work itself, and measuring yourself by real results. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Michael Eisner turned Disney around with his partner Frank Wells, but success went to his head: Euro Disney failed and he blamed Wells for it. After Wells died in a helicopter crash, Eisner fired Jeffrey Katzenberg and Michael Ovitz and pushed Roy Disney off the board, until Roy led a shareholder revolt, Eisner lost the chairmanship, and he resigned in 2005.

chapters.title: Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You: The Law of Gender Rigidity
chapters.keys:
Reconnect to the Masculine or Feminine Within You: The Law of Gender Rigidity
Everyone has both masculine and feminine qualities, and most people suppress the side that does not fit their gender role. That suppressed side does not vanish; it gets projected onto others, especially lovers, and makes you see them falsely. Greene borrows Carl Jung's terms for this inner opposite, the anima in men and the animus in women. Recognize your projections, reconnect with the side you have buried, and let both sides work in you; he argues this makes you more flexible, creative and complete. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Caterina Sforza, a Renaissance Italian noblewoman, drew on both sides of her nature, leading and fighting to hold her lands against powerful enemies.

chapters.title: Advance with a Sense of Purpose: The Law of Aimlessness
chapters.keys: Most people drift without a real aim and fill the gap with distractions. Find your calling, the work only you can do, and organize your life around it. Greene warns against false purposes: pleasure, causes and cults, money and success, attention, and cynicism. His strategies for building a high purpose: discover your calling; use resistance and setbacks as spurs; absorb the energy of purposeful people; build a ladder of smaller goals stepping down from your larger aim; and lose yourself in the work. A real purpose gives your life direction and makes you resilient when things go wrong. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Martin Luther King Jr., a young minister leading the Montgomery bus boycott, got a threatening phone call late at night, sat in his kitchen gripped by fear, and came out of that moment calm, with a sense of his mission.

chapters.title: Resist the Downward Pull of the Group: The Law of Conformity
chapters.keys: In a group, people lose their individual judgment and get pulled into the group's emotions, prejudices and pecking order. The urge to fit in, to belong, to be accepted makes you think and act in ways you never would alone. See how your group works, with its courtiers jostling for the favor of whoever holds power, without getting swept up in it. Keep your distance in your own mind, and if you lead, build what he calls a reality group, focused on real goals rather than politics, where ideas move freely and members are bound by shared work. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Gao Yuan, a student in Mao's China, and his friends, among them a devoted Maoist, were swept into the Cultural Revolution, which split them into warring factions.

chapters.title: Make Them Want to Follow You: The Law of Fickleness
chapters.keys: People are ambivalent toward their leaders; they want to follow and resent being led, and they turn on leaders quickly. Do not count on titles or position; earn authority, the kind of standing that makes people want to follow you. Greene's steps include finding your own authoritative style, turning your attention outward to what your people need, keeping your eye on the long term, leading by example from the front, and showing you put the group's interests above your own. Authority built this way, he says, lasts because people come to trust you and see you as acting for them. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Elizabeth I came to the English throne as a young woman whom many doubted, and built lasting authority by putting the realm's interests ahead of her own, spending carefully and leading by example.

chapters.title: See the Hostility Behind the Friendly Facade: The Law of Aggression
chapters.keys: Under the friendly surface, people carry aggression, and the most dangerous aggressors are the ones who hide it best. Greene calls them sophisticated aggressors: people who chase power and control relentlessly while presenting a calm or kindly face. Learn to read the signs, the pattern of past behavior, the hunger for control, the passive-aggressive moves that strike without showing it. Know the aggression in yourself too, and turn it into controlled aggression: ambition, persistence, fearlessness and anger used for good ends. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: John D. Rockefeller built Standard Oil by quietly and relentlessly crushing and swallowing competitors while presenting himself as a pious, mild man, until public anger and the government turned on his company.

chapters.title: Seize the Historical Moment: The Law of Generational Myopia
chapters.keys: You belong to a generation, and its outlook shapes you far more than you realize. Each generation reacts against the one before, and history moves in a cycle of such generations, each with its own spirit. Step back and see your own generation's blind spots and the larger pattern you live inside. Then use that knowledge: understand the spirit of the times and see where it is heading. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Georges-Jacques Danton sensed the desire for change in his time and rode it to power in the French Revolution.

chapters.title: Meditate on Our Common Mortality: The Law of Death Denial
chapters.keys: People avoid thinking about death, and that denial makes them live small, distracted and afraid. Face your mortality directly and use it to live more fully. Greene's steps: make death real to yourself; wake up to how short life is; see mortality in everyone around you, which binds you to them; embrace pain and adversity as part of life; and open your mind to the sublime, the vastness beyond yourself. He argues that awareness of death gives you urgency and focus and frees you from petty fears. Reversal: none. Story the author tells: Flannery O'Connor learned as a young woman that she had lupus, the disease that had killed her father, and that she would probably die young; she used that awareness to deepen her faith and write with great intensity until her death.
